questions.q: Why can't Solara-70B's checkpoint be saved as a single file the way a small model's checkpoint can?
options: S3 does not support files larger than a few megabytes

The model's weights are sharded across all 512 GPUs under FSDP, so gathering the full model onto one rank to write a single file would require that rank to hold the entire model's memory and create a serialization bottleneck
PyTorch does not support saving model weights to cloud storage
Single-file checkpoints are only supported for inference, not training
questions.explain: FSDP shards the model across GPUs so no single GPU holds the full model. Gathering it all onto one rank for a single-file save would require massive memory on that rank and turn the save into a slow sequential bottleneck.

questions.q: How does torch.distributed.checkpoint (DCP) avoid the single-rank bottleneck when saving a checkpoint?
options: It skips saving the optimizer state entirely to reduce size
Every rank saves only the shard of state it already holds, writing all shards to the checkpoint directory concurrently, with metadata describing how to reassemble them
It compresses the entire model into a smaller file before saving
It saves the checkpoint only once per day regardless of step count
questions.explain: DCP has each rank write its own already-held shard directly and in parallel with every other rank, avoiding any gather step and turning one huge sequential write into many small concurrent ones.

questions.q: Why does Solara AI checkpoint roughly every 500 steps (~30 minutes) instead of every single step or once a day?
options: 500 steps is an arbitrary PyTorch default that cannot be changed
It balances the overhead of checkpointing (which costs time if done every step) against the worst-case progress lost on failure (which grows large if checkpointing is too infrequent, like once a day)
S3 only accepts writes every 30 minutes
GPUs physically require a cooldown period of 30 minutes between writes
questions.explain: Checkpointing too frequently wastes GPU time on overhead; checkpointing too rarely means a failure can cost close to a full day of compute. A ~30-minute interval caps worst-case loss while keeping steady-state overhead small.

questions.q: Why does Solara AI write checkpoints to the S3 bucket solara-checkpoints rather than to each node's local disk?
options: Local disks on GPU nodes cannot be written to during training
A checkpoint on local disk is tied to that specific node's health, which defeats the purpose of a fault-tolerance mechanism meant to survive that very node failing
S3 is always faster to write to than local NVMe
AWS requires all training data to be stored in S3 by policy
questions.explain: If a checkpoint lived only on a node's local disk, losing that node to failure could also lose the checkpoint. S3 is durable and independent of any single node, including the one that might fail.

questions.q: What does the checkpoint metadata written by dcp.save enable that a plain collection of shard files without metadata would not?
options: Faster model inference after training completes
The ability to later load the checkpoint back onto a different number of GPUs than the run that originally saved it
Automatic compression of the checkpoint files
Encryption of the checkpoint data at rest
questions.explain: DCP's metadata describes how the shards map back onto the model and optimizer state, which is what allows dcp.load (covered in the next lesson) to resume training with a different GPU/world-size configuration than was used to save.
